assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with nominal rigidities, microfounded monetary models and policy-rule analysis, is the dominant working framework in academic and central-bank macroeconomics. It changed both theory and practice in monetary policy.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across eight listed names. A defensible core is the synthesis and normative policy theory (Woodford, Gali), the policy-rule contribution (Taylor), and Calvo pricing as an essential building block. Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets are largely estimated-DSGE implementers. Any three-person selection leaves out important contributors.
assessment.maturity: The work spans several decades, has been tested through inflation targeting, the financial crisis and the post-pandemic inflation, and is well confirmed. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Whether three names can capture the contribution without distorting the credit.
Whether the post-2021 inflation episode and heterogeneous-agent critiques reduce the prize case for the representative-agent framework.
My assessment relies on prior knowledge and no source was independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work built modern political economics: formal analysis of electoral rules, constitutions, fiscal outcomes and state capacity, joined to empirical tests. It has shaped public economics, comparative politics and development.
assessment.attribution: The core credit is clean, with the Persson-Tabellini research program and the Besley-Persson work on state capacity and development. It forms a natural three-person group.
assessment.maturity: The foundational contributions date from the 1990s and 2000s and are widely taught and replicated. Recent institutions-related recognition has partly covered adjacent ground, but the contribution here is distinct.
uncertainties: Possible perceived overlap with earlier recognition of institutions and political economy research.
Some structural political-economy predictions are harder to identify cleanly in the data than the headline theory suggests.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection transformed trade theory and empirics by shifting analysis from countries and industries to firms. It identified new gains-from-trade channels and underpins much current trade policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman's broader work on heterogeneous firms, trade and organisation complements it. Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions are important but more recent, so I leave him out of the proposed group.
assessment.maturity: The framework has been confirmed through two decades of firm-level data work and has become standard.
uncertainties: Contributions by Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and by Krugman's earlier work, complicate attribution.
Helpman is also credited in another trade ballot entry, so credit may be split.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data gave credible measurements of intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and the long-run value of policy. It changed how economists and policymakers study opportunity, and it applies the credibility-revolution approach at scale.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is clearly central. Hendren and Friedman are key co-developers of the mobility, neighbourhood and teacher-value-added work. Katz's contributions are better captured elsewhere on the list.
assessment.maturity: The main results are roughly a decade old. Replication and policy uptake are strong, though long-run follow-up is still developing.
uncertainties: Some causal interpretations of neighbourhood effects are still debated.
Whether the contribution is more data and measurement than conceptual framework is open to debate.
Chetty's work spans several ballot entries, which could blur the discovery boundary.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based approach to technology and the evidence on trade shocks and wage inequality reshaped understanding of labour demand, polarisation and adjustment costs. The work is empirically credible and policy-relevant.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task approach and the China-shock research. Katz has a long record on skill-biased demand shifts and the education-technology race. Hanson is a leading co-author on trade shocks. Dorn is a strong co-author but less central.
assessment.maturity: Findings from the 1990s on technology and the 2010s on trade shocks have been widely replicated, qualified and extended.
uncertainties: Debate continues on the size and persistence of the trade-shock effects and on whether the task framework fully explains inequality.
Overlap with the Goldin recognition on gender and labour history.
Credit boundaries, since the task framework involves non-listed co-originators.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral-constraint amplification shows how small shocks produce large and persistent credit cycles. It is a central mechanism in macro-finance and in policy thinking after the financial crisis.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) are the originators of the credit-cycle mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the related financial-accelerator work, but Bernanke's earlier role complicates credit for that branch, so the two-person proposal is cleaner.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly thirty years old and has been widely confirmed and extended. Financial-crisis recognition in 2022 covered related but distinct ground.
uncertainties: Perceived overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
Gertler also appears in the New Keynesian entry, so credit may be split.
Direct empirical identification of the amplification mechanism is harder than the theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run series on top incomes and wealth, built from tax and administrative records, reshaped the evidence base and public debate on inequality, and opened a large empirical literature. The data contribution is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the originators of the top-income data programme. Zucman extends it to wealth and offshore holdings. Credit for the datasets is shared with Atkinson and others, and Atkinson is not alive to be recognised.
assessment.maturity: The data work is established. The theoretical interpretation, such as r>g and its policy implications, is more contested and less confirmed.
uncertainties: Disputes over measurement choices, such as the treatment of pensions, transfers and taxes.
Whether the prize case rests on measurement or on explanatory theory.
Policy and political salience may colour the assessment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Alternating-offers bargaining gave a tractable non-cooperative foundation for bargaining and linked it to market outcomes through decentralised exchange. It is a core tool in theory and applied models.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the central contribution, and Rubinstein-Wolinsky on bargaining in markets is the natural complement. Binmore's contributions are important, especially the link to Nash bargaining, but are more of a secondary strand.
assessment.maturity: The results are over forty years old and thoroughly confirmed in theory. Their empirical and experimental footprint is less direct.
uncertainties: Perceived overlap with earlier game-theory and mechanism-design recognition.
Limited direct empirical validation compared with other candidates.
Stahl's related earlier work and Binmore's role raise attribution questions.
